The published Markov inequality is applied to the squared centered chi-square variable to prove convergence in probability.

The published theorem constructs the product measure for sigma-finite factors and states its rectangle formula. The interpolation proof uses a product probability space to realize independent Gaussian vectors with the required marginal laws.

The published theorem passes limits through integrals under an integrable common majorant. In the interpolation proof, difference quotients on compact subintervals are dominated by a constant times the integrable Euclidean norms of the Gaussian input vectors.

The published theorem applies to finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, gives the normal equations and nonempty affine minimizer set beta_0+ker X. The authored item uses its finite real Euclidean case and proves uniqueness iff ker X={0}.
The published definition fixes ||Ax-b||_2^2+lambda||x||_2^2 for lambda>0 over finite real or complex matrices. The authored ridge objective matches it exactly.
The published theorem supplies strict convexity and the formula (A^*A+lambda I)^-1A^*b for lambda>0. The authored item applies it to A=X,b=y and separately checks invertibility by the SVD spectrum.

The published SVD theorem covers finite-dimensional real or complex inner-product spaces and rank zero. The authored real-matrix case diagonalizes X^T X and verifies that adding lambda I gives positive eigenvalues.

The published definition assumes AC, allows positive-semidefinite covariance, and identifies Gaussian linear projections. The cex uses only the nonsingular identity-covariance specialization and finite linear transformations.

The published density theorem requires AC and a positive-definite covariance. It supplies the factorized standard Gaussian density used to verify orthogonal invariance and independence of coordinates in the block decomposition.
The published theorem makes the joint law of a finite independent family its product law. The cex uses this for independent observations, rows, and the rotated Gaussian coordinates.
The published sigma-finite product-measure theorem supplies an independent auxiliary Gaussian product factor for the finite maximum comparison in step 5.1.

The published concentration theorem gives exp(-r^2/(2L^2)) upper tails for L-Lipschitz functions of standard Gaussian vectors and explicitly assumes AC, DC, and countable choice. The cex applies it to minus the Gaussian coordinate maximum after the covariance-square-root representation.
AC is explicitly assumed for the Gaussian laws and concentration supplier. This dependency records the stated axiom, not an unstated implication.
DC is separately stated because the Gaussian Lipschitz concentration supplier assumes it.
